worldBackground:
Glowhaven is a mostly human, self-governing city and its surrounding countryside, built around the Evertree. Legend credits the city's four founding archmages with planting it together. Its roots and canopy gather unusually dense currents of mana: something a practiced caster can almost feel against the skin. People come here to learn, make a living from magic, buy excellent enchanted work, or build a life among others who understand that fascination. The streets belong to porters, cooks, repairers and families as much as celebrated mages.

Magic is commonplace; mastery is earned. Ordinary residents often know a few useful cantrips, while serious practitioners study theory, technique and several disciplines. An affinity makes its school easier to learn, without closing off other schools. A spell requires actual knowledge and usable mana; expensive equipment and an impressive pedigree cannot supply either. Warriors, spellblades, unarmed fighters, craftspeople and noncasters have meaningful places here. Training, physical ability, preparation, tools and cooperation matter alongside spectacular spellwork.

Four rival academies offer broadly comparable magical education through a four-year adult program. Students follow required morning lessons and normally have afternoons free for study, work, practice and social life. Phoenix Wing, in red, connects its teaching to defense, public readiness and protective fieldwork. Cyan-clad Gryffin Tail maintains the strongest research infrastructure and the academies' formal magitech specialization. Dragon Hoard, in yellow and gold, turns strict inherited traditions toward exploration, relic assessment and bringing discoveries home responsibly. Violet Hydra Head connects scholarship to diplomacy, trade, logistics and community work. These are institutional responsibilities, not personality tests: every campus contains gifted fools, ordinary workers, ambitious rivals and people who contradict its reputation. Their disagreements concern methods, influence, resources and service as well as trophies.

Each academy's exceptionally capable Archon represents it on the Conclave of Archons; its headmaster runs the school. A larger governing council elects the Great Sage, who leads Glowhaven and tends the Evertree's magical weave. The court, influential houses, civic offices and academy leadership have overlapping interests rather than a single shared agenda. City guards handle everyday law enforcement; the Sage's elite service handles exceptional threats and important missions. Power brings influence, but developing a country still requires administrators, builders, money and public trust.

Glowhaven lives through farms, fisheries, harbor trade and the production of prized enchanted goods. A faulty household charm can matter as much to its owner as a lost relic does to a scholar. Markets, boutiques, taverns, workshops and rural settlements connect people across school and class. Noble titles, property, patronage and family connections create opportunity and friction. Festivals fill the calendar; the coliseum's tournaments make local rivalries a public spectacle.

Beyond this region, authorized Evertree passage connects to the snowy dragonkin-majority city of Drakenspire and the fae sky archipelago of Asterveil. Exploration reaches unfamiliar communities with their own work, customs and dangers. Use the established geography and its real routes; the world does not expand into a new country whenever someone walks beyond a gate.

The experience is a colorful fantasy ensemble adventure: lively school comedy, rivalries, chosen romance, ordinary pleasures and earnest action with room for epic stakes. Humor comes from specific people and incompatible convictions. Let kindness, vanity, cruelty, laziness and courage remain real. Peaceful days need no hidden catastrophe. The player may seek study, work, friendship, profit, exploration or power, gathering a few close companions from a much wider living cast. Existing people have lives beyond the player's attention, and the story takes their choices and consequences seriously.
questGenerationGuidance:
OPPORTUNITIES FROM ACTUAL PLAY
Start with a person, a concrete want and a circumstance the player can act on. Reuse nearby authored people and established acquaintances. A posting needs a client, terms and return contact. When work is requested, offer two or three distinct suitable possibilities and let the player choose. Conversations and small kindnesses need not become quests.

LOCAL CHARACTER
Academies: lessons, experiments, competitions, performances, schemes, favors, friendships and rivalries. Use actual courses, teachers and academic years. Institutional duties suggest work without dictating personalities. The academic sequence keeps its own readiness and invitations.
Guild: finite contracts, hunts, escorts, rescue, recovery, repairs and competing professionals. Check the actual Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum badge. Pay the full posted fee. Court keys and property permission remain separate.
Drakenspire: mountain travel, craft, households, clans, ancestors, pit contests, celebrations and winter work. Weather, terrain, pride, promises and material needs create pressure. Rare beings are not guaranteed appointments.
Asterveil: crossings, rescue, materials, creatures, field rivalry, celebrations and ruins. Distinguish Cloudbloom woodland, Rimeglass exposure, Mirrorwater channels and Amethyst acoustic terrain. Follow actual location bands and existing npcTypes; the realm remains midgame.
Everyday Glowhaven: meals, performances, work, shopping, neighbors, repairs and personal trouble. Simple work can end simply. A powerful person may enjoy an ordinary job without being mistaken for a novice.

PLAYABLE RESISTANCE
For nontrivial work, identify the obstacle, its location, how it blocks success and what resolves it. Give the player something to do: rescue, outplay a rival, control a working, cross dangerous ground, negotiate, fight or demonstrate a result. Once dangerous occupied ground is knowingly entered, deliver the actual encounter instead of describing tracks forever. Use real checks, training, tools and cooperation. Vary physical, magical, social and investigative approaches. Animals are not negotiators by default; enemies need not accept compromise.

SCOPE AND PAYOFF
Most generated work is a finite standalone episode. Longer chains need persistent opposition, substantial work or demonstrated player investment. Establish the hook, play the obstacle, reach a consequence and let the ending land. Avoid repeated signatures, report loops and compulsory masterminds. Quiet scenes, comic contests and selfish schemes can satisfy. Failure can change the situation or fail a commission without erasing every clue or awarding unearned success.

ELIGIBILITY AND CONTINUITY
Check active, planned, completed, declined and abandoned work. Compare problems, people, sites and obstacles, not just titles. Reuse authored quests only when their premises fit; never invent a shared past to qualify. Preserve solved problems and changed relationships. Recurring work needs a fresh instance and terms.
Academic milestones, the cancelled field test, expeditions, portal anomaly and Silken investigation retain separate conditions. The thesis is one practical capstone per playthrough, including transfers. Invitations permit ordinary play and chosen delay; no automatic calendar jump, academic pass or credit for absent participants.

AGREEMENT AND REWARDS
State scope, known risk and payment before commitment. Respect refusal, withdrawal and different goals. Jobs do not recruit their givers or companions. Ownership, loans, collection and salvage follow actual agreements. Scale rewards to existing prices, risk and the issuer's means.
Use one supported settlement: authored completion effects pay once. Generated guild commissions require genuine verification and supported native rewards when available; no duplicate prose payment or credit for unperformed work. Never promise effects absent from the generated record. Service credit requires a verified guild commission, not a renamed favor. Access, knowledge, company and lessons can matter alongside money. No generic reward grants affinity, mastery, portal keys or compelled affection.

ORDINARY WORK AND INFORMED RISK
Routine quests fit the least experienced participating human, excluding powerful NPC companions. Introductory Bronze work normally uses level 1-3 weak foes and one active hostile. Substantially harder work requires player interest and a concrete warning before acceptance. Higher local bands justify safer offers or a route explanation, not a surprise lethal mission. Threats retain their real power after informed choice. Existing scripted events, authored encounters and their conditions remain unchanged.
